title: Reproducibility and Limits
text:
What is fixed
Every analysis choice lives in params.yaml, which the scripts read. The table shows the main ones.


Show the code
w <- function(n) paste(range(pp("windows", n)), collapse = "–")
tab <- data.frame(
  Setting = c("Random seed", "Windows: classifier / overlay fit / overlay test",
              "Score sharpening", "Risk-band boundaries", "Resampling draws",
              "Trimming rule", "Deletion budget", "Significance level"),
  Value = c(pp("seed"), sprintf("%s / %s / %s", w("classifier_train"), w("calibration_fit"), w("overlay_eval")),
            pp("vendorscore", "sharpen"), sprintf("%s, %s", pct(pp("calibration", "band_low_upper"), 0), pct(pp("calibration", "band_medium_upper"), 0)),
            format(pp("calibration", "bootstrap_draws"), big.mark = ","), sprintf("top %s of patch latency", pct(1 - pp("fragility", "trim_percentile"), 0)),
            pp("fragility", "deletion_budget"), pct(pp("fragility", "alpha"), 0)),
  Basis = c("assumption", "assumption", "planted", "assumption", "convention", "assumption", "assumption", "convention"))
knitr::kable(tab)

title: Reproducibility and Limits
text:
Limitations

Synthetic data. Confounding, regime shift and overconfidence are planted. Real use needs NorthPoint’s vendor-month panel, incident definition and dated SOC 2 reports.
Few events. 75 evaluation incidents and 18 forecast months limit power; more history could change pages 2 and 3.
Thin overlay window. Six months and 28 incidents is little. A real overlay needs a refit schedule and tolerances set in advance.
Information timing. Start-of-month availability of patch latency and financial health is assumed; real feeds need timestamps.
One dataset. Seed 34 was chosen in development; the seed sweep on page 4 checks repeatability only.
Partial validation. Scores and outcomes only; the vendor’s internals stay unseen.

title: Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?
text: Does VendorScore forecast NorthPoint’s monthly incident total better than a plain 12-month rolling average of past counts, and does any advantage survive the deterioration in vendor patching after month 36? This tests one use of the model, aggregate monthly count forecasting. VendorScore may have other value, such as ranking vendors for attention, which this comparison does not price.

title: Three Questions for Any Risk Model
text:
The decision problem
Your bank pays a vendor for a number. Every month, a model called VendorScore hands NorthPoint Bank a risk score for each of its 300 third-party vendors. Nobody at the bank can see the code, the training data, or the method. The scores arrive, and decisions follow.
How do you validate something you cannot open? This project shows how much can be learned from the scores and what happens afterwards, and where outside testing stops.


The three questions
The April 17, 2026 interagency Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC) is explicitly non-prescriptive. We read it as describing sound practice, not rules. The three questions below are this project’s practical interpretation, not a regulator-prescribed checklist. Each works on any risk model.
Reading the § marks. § means “section.” Pages cite these parts of the guidance:

§III, overview of model risk: what makes a model risky, how much a model matters (materiality), and independent critical review (“effective challenge”).
§IV, development and use: how models are built and tested, and the risk of using a model for something it was not designed for.
§V, validation and monitoring: checking a model against real outcomes, watching it over time, and adjusting, recalibrating or rebuilding it if needed.
§VI, governance and controls: policies, roles and records, including documenting exceptions.
§VII, vendor products: applying the same discipline to bought models whose code and data the bank may never see.


Are its probabilities honest? When the model says 10%, do incidents happen about 10% of the time? This is calibration, tested with probcal (Page 2).
Does it beat a simple model? A sophisticated model should outperform a plain 12-month average, and keep doing so when conditions change. This is forecast dominance, tested with forecastdom (Page 3).
Would its headline finding survive a push? Some findings collapse under a small change of method or data. This is fragility, tested with falsifyr (Page 4).







Figure 1: Each test is tied to a question and to the decision it protects.




How to read the plot. Each of the three columns is one question. Reading down, each column shows the question, the test, and the decision it protects.
What the plot tells you. A model can pass one test and fail another, so one test alone leaves two decisions unprotected.







NoteMateriality box (illustrative ratings)



Judging how much validation a model deserves (guidance §III) looks at three things:

Inherent risk: high. VendorScore is opaque, its assumptions and data are hidden, and vendor incidents are rare events, which limits the data available to test it.
Exposure: broad. The score covers all 300 vendors in the portfolio.
Purpose: consequential. Scores inform monitoring intensity and contract terms.

Exposure and purpose together determine materiality, assessed alongside inherent risk. Illustrative conclusion: full validation is warranted.




The case
NorthPoint Bank is a fictional regional bank with about $45 billion in assets. The guidance is expected to be most relevant to banks above $30 billion; some smaller banks may also find it relevant. Asset managers and fintechs fall outside its scope but can adopt similar practices voluntarily.
All pages share one synthetic dataset: 14,400 vendor-months (300 vendors over 48 months, January 2022 to December 2025), with 209 observed incidents, or 1.45% of vendor-months. Because the data are simulated, we know each vendor-month’s true incident probability, used only as a reference; the models never see it. Everything is reproducible from seed 34.
A fictional vendor, RiskMetric Systems, supplies VendorScore, trained on months 1 to 30. NorthPoint fits a recalibration overlay on months 31 to 36 and assesses it on months 37 to 48 (Page 2). Page 3 compares the raw scores with a benchmark over months 31 to 48, a period that includes a deterioration in vendors’ patching speed after month 36.


The black-box problem
Guidance on vendor products (§VII) recognises that a bank may lack access to a vendor model’s inner workings. The vendor’s summary offers only “ensemble machine learning on proprietary threat intelligence,” an AUC of 0.81 “on vendor development data,” and the assertion that scores are “well-calibrated.”
The bank can evaluate how the scores perform on its own outcomes, for calibration and discrimination. It cannot reproduce the vendor’s development-data AUC or inspect the hidden development choices. Testing scores against outcomes is partial validation only: it cannot confirm that the proprietary model is conceptually sound. That depends on what the vendor discloses (§VII).


How to read this project
Pages 2 to 4 share one structure: the question, the method in brief, the findings, what they mean for the bank, and one committee action phrased as “sound practice suggests…”. The expected findings were written as hypotheses before any analysis ran; where a result differs, the text reports the result. Code is folded by default. Page 4 closes with a scorecard of measured results; a final page covers reproducibility and limits.

title: Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?
text: When VendorScore says a vendor has a 10% chance of an incident, do incidents happen about 10% of the time? RiskMetric Systems asserts that its scores are “well-calibrated.” NorthPoint cannot inspect the model, but it can compare the scores with what happened, and it can test whether a recalibration overlay would help.

title: Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?
text: NorthPoint built its own logistic regression, the bank’s incident-association model, from its panel. Its headline: vendors without a current SOC 2 Type II report have about twice the odds of an incident (odds ratio 2.04, vendor-clustered 95% interval 1.48 to 2.82). That finding now supports a contract policy. How small a change makes it disappear?

title: Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?
text:
Actionable Insights
Sound practice suggests documenting the SOC 2 finding as an exception (§VI) and analysing its new use before relying on it (§IV). Do not use this association alone to infer the effect of requiring SOC 2: contract requirements need business, legal and control evidence. The guidance does not prescribe this.
